isolated-neutral-system: An isolated neutral system is a power system that has no intentional connection to earth, except through indicating, measuring or protective devices of very high impedance ([[iec-56]] 3.101.5). Because there is no deliberate low-impedance neutral-to-earth path, single phase-to-earth faults drive only small capacitive currents through the line-to-earth capacitances rather than large fault currents. The trade-off is that the sound (healthy) phases rise close to full line-to-line voltage relative to earth during an earth fault, giving a high [[earth-fault-factor]] approaching the square root of 3. This contrasts with the [[earthed-neutral-system]], where the neutral is deliberately bonded to earth, and with the [[resonant-earthed-system]], which uses an arc-suppression coil. The earthing arrangement directly governs the [[earth-fault-factor]] and hence the [[external-insulation]] and [[internal-insulation]] stresses the circuit-breaker must withstand.
resonant-earthed-system: A resonant earthed system (also called a system earthed through an arc-suppression coil) is one in which the neutral is earthed through a reactor whose reactance is tuned so that, during a single phase-to-earth fault, the power-frequency inductive current passed by the reactor substantially neutralizes the power-frequency capacitive component of the earth-fault current ([[iec-56]] 3.101.6). This Petersen-coil tuning cancels the line-to-earth capacitive current, so the residual current in the fault is limited to such an extent that an arcing fault in air is usually self-extinguishing. Like the [[isolated-neutral-system]] it limits earth-fault current, but it does so by inductive compensation rather than absence of a path. It sits between the [[isolated-neutral-system]] and the [[earthed-neutral-system]] in earthing philosophy; the resulting [[earth-fault-factor]] is high, influencing required insulation and the [[recovery-voltage]] across the breaker.
earthed-neutral-system: An earthed neutral system is one in which the neutral is connected to earth, either solidly, or through a resistance or reactance of a value low enough to reduce materially any transient oscillations and to improve the conditions for selective earth-fault protection ([[iec-56]] 3.101.7). By providing a low-impedance neutral path, it holds the sound phases close to their normal phase-to-earth voltage during an earth fault, yielding a comparatively low [[earth-fault-factor]] — not exceeding 1.4 when the zero-sequence reactance is below three times the positive-sequence reactance and zero-sequence resistance does not exceed positive-sequence reactance ([[iec-56]] 3.101.8). This contrasts with the [[isolated-neutral-system]] and the [[resonant-earthed-system]], both of which limit earth-fault current but allow sound-phase voltages to rise toward the square root of 3. The lower earth-fault factor permits reduced [[external-insulation]] and [[rated-insulation-level]] for the same nominal system voltage.
earth-fault-factor: The earth fault factor, at a selected location of a three-phase system (generally the point of installation of equipment) and for a given system configuration, is the ratio of the highest r.m.s. phase-to-earth power-frequency voltage on a sound phase during a fault to earth (affecting one or more phases at any point) to the r.m.s. phase-to-earth power-frequency voltage that would be obtained at the same location without the fault ([[iec-56]] 3.101.8). It is a pure numerical ratio greater than 1 characterizing the earthing conditions of the system as viewed from that location, independent of actual operating voltage. It equals the square root of 3 times the older factor of earthing, and is computed from the phase-sequence impedance components using subtransient reactances for rotating machines. It will not exceed 1.4 in an effectively [[earthed-neutral-system]], but approaches the square root of 3 in an [[isolated-neutral-system]] or [[resonant-earthed-system]]; this factor sets the sound-phase overvoltage that determines the required [[rated-insulation-level]].
external-insulation: External insulation comprises the distances in air and the surfaces of solid insulation of the equipment in contact with open air, which are subject to dielectric stresses and to the effects of atmospheric and other external conditions such as pollution, humidity, vermin, etc. ([[iec-56]] 3.101.20). Because it is exposed to the environment, its dielectric strength is influenced by air density, moisture and surface contamination, and discharges across it are typically flashover (over a solid surface) or sparkover (in air). It is therefore generally [[self-restoring-insulation]], recovering full insulating strength after a disruptive discharge, in contrast to the [[internal-insulation]] which is shielded from external conditions and may be [[non-self-restoring-insulation]]. Together external and internal insulation define the dielectric withstand expressed by the [[rated-insulation-level]] of the circuit-breaker.
internal-insulation: Internal insulation consists of the internal solid, liquid or gaseous parts of the insulation of equipment, which are protected from the effects of atmospheric and other external conditions ([[iec-56]] 3.101.21). Being shielded from pollution, humidity and weather, its performance is governed by the intrinsic dielectric strength of the enclosed media rather than by ambient conditions. A disruptive discharge in a solid internal dielectric produces permanent loss of strength, making such insulation [[non-self-restoring-insulation]], whereas a discharge in an enclosed liquid or gaseous dielectric may recover, making it [[self-restoring-insulation]] ([[iec-56]] 3.101.24, Note 2). It complements the [[external-insulation]], which is exposed to open air; the combined withstand capability of both is expressed by the equipment's [[rated-insulation-level]].
self-restoring-insulation: Self-restoring insulation is insulation which completely recovers its insulating properties after a disruptive discharge ([[iec-56]] 3.101.22). A disruptive discharge is a phenomenon associated with failure of insulation under electric stress in which the discharge completely bridges the insulation and reduces the voltage between electrodes to zero or nearly zero ([[iec-56]] 3.101.24). In liquid or gaseous dielectrics the loss of dielectric strength may be only temporary, so such media are typically self-restoring; this is why much [[external-insulation]] (air clearances, where discharges appear as flashover or sparkover) behaves this way. It contrasts directly with [[non-self-restoring-insulation]], which does not fully recover. The distinction matters for testing philosophy: self-restoring insulation tolerates repeated disruptive-discharge tests, and its withstand contributes to the [[rated-insulation-level]].
non-self-restoring-insulation: Non-self-restoring insulation is insulation which loses its insulating properties, or does not recover them completely, after a disruptive discharge ([[iec-56]] 3.101.23). A disruptive discharge completely bridges the insulation under electric stress, reducing the inter-electrode voltage to near zero ([[iec-56]] 3.101.24). In a solid dielectric a disruptive discharge — termed a puncture — produces permanent loss of dielectric strength, so solid internal insulation is generally non-self-restoring ([[iec-56]] 3.101.24, Note 2). This is the direct opposite of [[self-restoring-insulation]], which fully recovers. It is characteristic of much [[internal-insulation]], particularly solid parts shielded from external conditions, whereas [[external-insulation]] in air is usually self-restoring. Because each disruptive discharge is potentially destructive, withstand verification toward the [[rated-insulation-level]] uses non-destructive withstand tests rather than repeated breakdown.
rated-value: A rated value is a quantity value assigned, generally by a manufacturer, for a specified operating condition of a component, device or equipment ([[iec-56]] 3.105.1, IEV 151-04-03). It is the reference figure a circuit-breaker is designed and guaranteed to meet, so that the breaker in correct condition of maintenance and adjustment can withstand all service stresses provided they do not exceed its rated characteristics ([[iec-56]] clause 4). The standard enumerates the rated characteristics that define the rating, including rated voltage, [[rated-insulation-level]], rated frequency, rated normal current, rated short-time and peak withstand currents, rated short-circuit breaking and making currents, rated transient [[recovery-voltage]] for terminal faults, and rated operating sequence ([[iec-56]] clause 4). Each such rated characteristic is a specific instance of the general rated-value concept defined here.
prospective-current: The prospective current (of a circuit, with respect to a circuit-breaker) is the current that would flow in the circuit if each pole of the circuit-breaker were replaced by a conductor of negligible impedance ([[iec-56]] 3.105.2, IEV 441-17-01). It therefore represents the current the circuit itself can deliver, determined by the source and circuit impedances alone and independent of the limiting effect of the actual breaker. It is the reference quantity from which several rated and test quantities are derived: the [[prospective-peak-current]] is the peak value of its first major loop during the transient period following initiation ([[iec-56]] 3.105.3), and the prospective breaking current is the prospective current evaluated at the instant the arc is initiated during breaking ([[iec-56]] 3.105.9). Related notions include prospective symmetrical current and prospective making current ([[iec-56]] 3.105.5, 3.105.7).
prospective-peak-current: The prospective peak current is the peak value of the first major loop of the [[prospective-current]] during the transient period following initiation ([[iec-56]] 3.105.3). The definition assumes the current is made by an ideal circuit-breaker — one with instantaneous and simultaneous transition of its pole impedance from infinity to zero across the terminals of each pole. The peak value may differ from one pole to another because it depends on the instant of current initiation relative to the voltage wave across each pole's terminals; the asymmetry of this first loop is what makes it a peak rather than the symmetrical r.m.s. value. It parallels the (peak) making current, which is the corresponding peak in an actual pole during a making operation ([[iec-56]] 3.105.8), and relates to the maximum prospective peak current of an a.c. circuit ([[iec-56]] 3.105.6).
recovery-voltage: The recovery voltage is the voltage that appears across the terminals of a pole of a circuit-breaker after the breaking of the current ([[iec-56]] 3.105.23, IEV 441-17-25). It is conventionally considered in two successive intervals: an initial transient period, during which the [[transient-recovery-voltage]] (TRV) may exist, followed by a second period during which only the power-frequency recovery voltage exists ([[iec-56]] 3.105.24, 3.105.26). This voltage is what stresses the contact gap immediately after arc extinction at current zero; if it rises faster than the gap regains dielectric strength, the result is a [[reignition]] (within a quarter-cycle of current zero) or a [[restrike]] (a quarter-cycle or more after current zero). The rated transient recovery voltage for terminal faults is one of the circuit-breaker's defining rated characteristics ([[iec-56]] clause 4).
restrike: A restrike is a resumption of current between the contacts of a switching device during a breaking operation occurring a quarter of a cycle of power frequency or more after the most recent current zero ([[iec-56]] 3.105.47, IEV 441-17-46). The quarter-cycle timing is the defining threshold that distinguishes it from a [[reignition]], which occurs less than a quarter-cycle after current zero ([[iec-56]] 3.105.46). A restrike therefore represents a dielectric failure of the gap relatively late, after the [[recovery-voltage]] (and its transient component, the TRV) has built up to a substantial value, making restrikes particularly significant in capacitive switching where they can generate escalating overvoltages. A breaker designed to avoid them is termed restrike-free ([[iec-56]] 3.102.12). Restrike behaviour is closely tied to the rate of rise of the [[recovery-voltage]] versus the dielectric recovery of the gap.
reignition: A reignition is a resumption of current between the contacts of a switching device during a breaking operation occurring less than a quarter of a cycle of power frequency after the most recent current zero ([[iec-56]] 3.105.46, IEV 441-17-45). The sub-quarter-cycle timing is precisely what distinguishes it from a [[restrike]], which occurs a quarter-cycle or more after current zero ([[iec-56]] 3.105.47). Because a reignition happens so soon after current zero, the [[recovery-voltage]] across the gap is still low, so it is generally far less onerous than a restrike and does not by itself cause the overvoltage escalation associated with late dielectric failures. Both phenomena describe the gap failing to hold off the rising [[recovery-voltage]] after arc extinction; the quarter-cycle boundary between them is the key classifying criterion for assessing interruption performance.
